speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, May 14, consideration of the motion of the Minister of Finance that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself again into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Ralston.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Before the debate is
resumed, I think it would be well to give a ruling on the question of order raised yesterday by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) as to whether the amendment to the motion is in order. On April 23rd, Mr. Ralston moved as an amendment to the motion of the Minister of Finance that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself again into committee of ways and means, the following:
This house regrets that the proposals of the Minister of Finance give no indication of the intention of the government to abandon the policies of economic nationalism which have proved so disastrous to Canada's trade. It is of the opinion that the immediate substitution therefor of policies which will promote export trade throughout the world is essential to any permanent improvement of conditions in Canada, and to the successful application of other policies respecting credit and employment designed to effect this end.
On April 30, Mr. Spencer moved a subamendment and on May 7 on a question of order raised by Mr. Mackenzie, of Vancouver Centre, as to the subamendment, I held that the subamendment was not in order as it sought to deal with the question of credit which had been debated on a motion by Mr. Lucas and the matter of credit had been by consent referred to the select standing committee on banking and commerce where it is being considered.
It is now argued that the amendment is not in order and for the same reasons as said subamendment was held to be not in order.
When this amendment was moved, there was on the order paper Bill 51 entitled, "An Act to Improve the Methods and Practices of Marketing of Natural Products in Canada and in Export Trade, and to make further provision in connection therewith." This bill was read a first time March 26 and on April 23, when this amendment was moved, was on the order paper for second reading. The bill provides for export trade and for regulating the export of goods from Canada. See the title; and paragraph (b) of subsection 4; and paragraph (f) of subsection 5 of section 5; also section 12, subsection 2.
."Mr. Duranleau.]
On February 13, Mr. Woodsworth moved the following amendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne:
That the following be added to the motion:
We respectfully regret that Your Excellency's present advisers have not taken such steps as are necessary to deal adequately with unemployment, to reduce the burden imposed by tire public debt, and to put the agricultural industry on a basis that will ensure the farmer a decent standard of living.
Thereupon, employment was discussed and the amendment was disposed of by the house on a division resulting in 54 yeas and 89 nays.
That amendment dealt with the question of employment generally and the amendment now before the house is to the same effect and so is not in order.
My decision is supported by the following precedents. Bourinot, page 328:
"It is, however, an ancient Tule of parliament that no question or motion can be regularly offered if it is substantially the same with one on which the judgment of the house has already been expressed during the current session." The old rule of parliament reads: "That a question being once made, and carried in the affirmative or negative, cannot be questioned again, but must stand as a judgment of the house."
May, 13th edition, at page 272 says:
A matter already appointed for consideration by the house cannot be anticipated by an amendment, while a notice of motion as long as it remains upon the paper whether for a specified day or not, prevents its subject matter being discussed by means of an amendment to a motion.
Speaker's rulings on the question are reported as follows:
207 II.D. 3 s 500:
Now there is a rule of the house that when a matter has been expressly set down for consideration, no hon. member can anticipate it by raising a discussion on the subject.
308 H.D. 3 s 1755:
I must point out to the hon. member that he has introduced a bill, which is now standing on the paper for the second reading, which contains a distinct reference to the subject matter of the present motion; and, as that bill is to be brought on upon a future day, the hon. member would not be in order in moving his resolution now, as he would be anticipating the discussion upon the bill.
333 H.D. 3 s 851:
The first two amendments on the paper, the first standing in the name of the hon. member for Iloxton, and the second in that of the hon. baronet the member for Coekermouth, are out of order as amendments, inasmuch as they anticipate the discussion, one on three and the other on four bills which the house has appointed for a future day, and one of those bills, I observe, is in the name of the hon. gentleman himself. The amendment, therefore, of the hon. gentleman will be out of order as an amendment to the address.

The Budget-Speaker's Ruling
66 Parliamentary Debates, 4 s page 923:
The subject of the hon. member's amendment to the address is relative to several bills on the order book and he will have an opportunity of submitting his views to the house when one of them comes on. He cannot now anticipate discussion on a bill which is on the order book.
The same practice has always been followed in Canada, see Bourinot, 4th edition, page 320:
An amendment cannot anticipate a notice of motion on the order paper.
In this case the amendment goes further and anticipates a bill No. 51, now being considered in committee dealing with marketing and export trade.
I therefore rule that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) is out of order, as it is substantially the same as one on which the judgment of the house has already been expressed and it deals with matters already before the house.

The Budget-Mr. Manion

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this house met late in January and it is now the middle of May, so for the better part of four months we have been having discussions in the house as to the various measures which have been brought down by the government. During that time we have had a very great deal of fault finding and carping criticism, particularly on the part of the Liberal opposition. Their type of speeches might well be illustrated by the speeches delivered by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) on the address, which took some four and a half hours, and the speech of the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) on the budget, which took the better part of two and a half hours. In other words, those two speeches lasted for some seven hours, yet after a fairly thorough and somewhat painful reading of those speeches I have not been able to find one constructive suggestion advanced with the exception of the proposal by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth that we should have a refunding operation to cut down the interest rates in our country.
I wish to be entirely fair; the hon. member did make that constructive suggestion, but that proposal has been advanced by many members of this house. I think I have heard at least half a dozen members on this side deal with that matter, and that is something which all fair minded men must consider worthy of deep thought. To-day in Canada we have interest payments, if you include the Canadian National for which we are responsible. totalling $200,000,000 per annum in round figures, a stupendous burden to be placed on the backs of ten million people. The immensity of that burden can be realized even more clearly if it is remembered that it was not until 1910 that the federal revenues of the Dominion of Canada reached 1100,000,000, and at that time we had a population of seven million people. Of course, Mr. Speaker, we usually understand that it is the duty of an opposition to oppose, but at the same time during periods of national crisis in this and other parliaments sometimes it has been the custom of oppositions to rise to greater heights than that. But if you, sir, or anyone else can show me anything, other than the one constructive suggestion I have mentioned, that has been advanced by the present opposition during the four years we have been in power, any suggestion which took into account their country in its hour of trial rather than party politics, I should be very much obliged.
At that, Mr. Speaker, my chief criticism of the opposition at the present time is that whether it is on the address or on the budget, in their severe criticism of us they have entirely ignored world conditions. This country, in common with the rest of the world, has been going through four years of industrial and economic crisis, the worst the world has ever known. I do not give that as a mere figure of speech; I think it is a statement of fact. We have had an unemployment problem in the industrial countries of the world affecting some thirty million people, thirteen million of them in the great, powerful, rich country to the south where, in addition, they have had thousands of banks close their doors to their depositors. Practically all the countries of Europe, and certainly all those which took part in the war, have been unable to pay the interest on their war debts. We have had Fascist dictators spring up in six or eight of the prominent countries of Europe, with a dictatorship of the proletariat in Russia, where communism and starvation have been stalking together throughout the land. Even in South America, where they have no war debts, most of the republics have been unable to pay the interest on their national debts, and away over in the far east we have had threats of war which have endangered the peace of the world. In addition to all this we have had a condition of economic nationalism spring up throughout the world, in the last ten or fifteen years, all of which makes up a chaotic picture which is painful to consider, and of which Canada has been forced to become a part.
Due to world conditions we have had our serious unemployment problem in proportion to the unemployment that has existed throughout the world. In addition we have had a drought condition throughout the prairie provinces which in Saskatchewan alone a year or two ago threw one-third of the entire population upon relief. We find that the world price of wheat dropped to such an extent that the purchasing power of the prairie provinces decreased to an amount something like $450,000,000-a huge amount for that or for any other section of the country. In addition to that they have been unable, because of the world price of wheat, to pay their taxes, and therefore the western provinces-and in this I should add British Columbia-the four western provinces in avoiding default have indeed been dependent for financial assistance upon the Dominion of Canada. Then, added to all that, is the fact, which hon. members opposite ignore on all

The Budget-Mr. Manion

occasions, that the chaotic condition which in a few brief sentences I have described started before they went out of power. In fact, it started nearly a year before they went out of power, because it began after the crash in October of 1929. Yet, in their criticisms of this government, they never refer to world conditions, nor do they even admit that such conditions have existed.
Our record is open for all to read. I think it is a very good one, and in a few brief sentences I am going to cover the work of this government in its term of office, which has extended about four years. In the first place we realized that economies must be put into effect in Canada, and with that in mind we put those economies into effect to an amount of something like $81,000,000 per annum, cutting down the per capita cost of government in this country from $9.60 in the year before the war to $9.03 last year. We spent large sums of money on public works; we assisted the provinces, municipalities and the railways in their work of relieving unemployment, and we gave direct relief running into a large amount of money. We lent money by tens of millions to the western provinces. We saved the savings bank of the province of Manitoba; we gave a wheat bonus to the wheat growers of the western provinces. All of these actions of ours cost the government of Canada and the people of Canada something in the neighbourhood of $180,000,000. But as a result there has been no starvation in Canada, while in the only socialistic country in the world millions starve. We have maintained sound credit not only of the dominion, but of the provinces and the railways. We have saved their credit.
Then, so far as trade is concerned, we have held our own. We took part in two imperial conferences at which, for the first time in our history, we obtained preferences, profitable preferences-profitable to us and profitable to the other portions of the empire. It is true that the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) and other hon. members, have criticized my right hon. leader for having bargained to get those preferences. So far as I am concerned I am proud of the fact that my right hon. leader bargained, and I am proud of the fact that for the first time in our history we were on the receiving end instead of always being on the giving end.	.
Then, so far as world trade is concerned we must realize that there has been a serious decrease in the trade of all commercial countries of the world. So much is that true that

total world trade decreased from sixty-eight billion dollars in 1929 to twenty-six billion dollars in 1932, or about 60 per cent. Great Britain, one of the great trading nations, has had a decrease in her world trade in 1932 compared with 1929, amounting to five billion dollars, the United States six billion dollars, and Canada something like one and one-third billion dollars. So that Canada's decrease in trade, for which we have been criticized, has been in proportion to the decrease in the trade of all the other countries of the world, and of the world in general. In other words, we held our own, and last year our domestic exports went up $106,000,000 as compared with the year before, and our imports increased by $27,000,000. Yet in his speech sometime ago the hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth accused us of having "shackled world trade." He accused us not only once but a number of times. He said that "Canada had begun an economic nationalism." Well, the facts are that economic nationalism and the shackling of world trade began while my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition and his government were in power. As a matter of fact, the main shackling which has taken place, so far as Canada is concerned, was between the years 1925 and 1930, when a Liberal government was in power.
For example, let us take wheat. It has been pointed out many times that until 1929 wheat was allowed free into many European countries, but that in that year, the one before my right hon. friend left office, Italy, France and Germany raised the duty on wheat to 73 cents, 85 cents and 98 cents respectively per bushel. The truth is that the shackling of world trade and the economic nationalism which have taken place are due to war psychology which has existed since the war, particularly in European countries. It is due to the fact that many of those European countries have the fear of future wars, and are desirous of becoming self-sufficient so that in case of war they will be able to maintain themselves without importing from other countries. But the fact remains that so far as Europe is concerned that shackling took place in years of a Liberal administration in Canada. So far as the United States is concerned, anybody who reads political history or follows the affairs of Canada will know that between the years 1921 and 1930, when the Liberal government was in office the United States put up practically prohibitory tariffs against Canadian farm products. So

The Budget-Mr. Manion
much is that true, Mr. Speaker, that while in 1921, the first year of the Liberal regime, the United States imported $160,000,000 worth of Canadian farm products, in the last year in which the Liberal government held office the United States imported only $40,000,000 worth, or exactly one-quarter. And what was the attitude of my hon. friends opposite? What was the attitude of the present leader of the opposition? What was the attitude of that party when it was in power? It was unable to do anything. The leader of the opposition did not wish "to provoke the United States." As a matter of fact nothing was done by the Liberal government to increase the trade with the European countries and with the United States, or to decrease the tariffs which were rapidly being put up against the Dominion of Canada.
The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth also saw fit to belittle the balance of trade about which, I believe, we may justly boast a little. It must be remembered that Canada's external interest payments, including dominion, provincial, municipal and corporate, amount to something more than $200,000,000 yearly. That money has to go from this country every year. That interest can be paid only in goods, or by borrowing money. But borrowing in the last few years has not been very popular or convenient. With interest being payable in goods I should like to ask the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth or in fact any other hon. member, this question: How can any debtor country-meaning a country which must pay to outside countries more than they return in interest or debts-pay its outside debts if it imports more goods than it exports? It is absolutely essential, if we are to pay such debts, that we must export more than we import. Fortunately the balance of trade which when hon. members opposite left office was very markedly against us, in fact to the extent of $103,000,000, has been changed to a balance in our favour. In other words, in 1930, we bought $103,000,000 more of goods from outside countries than those outside countries bought from us. Last year we had a reverse condition, when we sold to the outside world $152,000,000 more than we bought from it, making a total change in trade figures of $255,000,000, plus gold amounting to something like $90,000,000, most of which we also exported.
That, in a very brief way is the record of this government. But in addition to that, at the present session we have placed before the house a marketing bill, a bill establishing a central bank, a mortgage bill protecting the

farmer and a public works program. Those are pieces of legislation which come to my mind at the moment. Therefore, generally speaking I submit that Canada's affairs have been handled better during this time of crisis throughout the world than have the affairs of any other country in the world, and I say that our condition at the present time is at least equal to that of any other country in the world, and in that statement I make no exception.
Does any sane man on the opposition side suggest that had the right hon. gentleman opposite been in power he could have handled the affairs of Canada during this economic hurricane in a better manner than they have been handled by the present government?

speechtext: Sure.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Some hon. members opposite cheer. I do not know whether they are the sane group or not. At any rate, Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask them this question: Could their leader or their party, had they been in power, have cured the drought in western Canada? Could they have controlled world wheat prices? Could they have stopped ultra-nationalism or economic nationalism which has grown up, and which was growing up during the nine years hon. members held office? Could they have cured unemployment? Could they have changed world conditions so that Canada would have held a better position or would have been in a better position than she has been in the past four years under a Conservative government? All we have to do is to look over the record of the Liberal party when they were in power and since they have been in opposition. In the four years they have been in opposition their whole record has been one of opposition to everything-opposition to the relief acts for weeks at a time, so much so that the western provinces on one or two occasions were unable to get their seed grain in time.

their leader at any rate has denied that conditions have improved in this country. They have capitalized discontent at every opportunity. They have done everything in their power even to destroying national optimism, apparently with no other object than to achieve power which they boast they would be able to do should an election be held at the present time.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the tactics of my hon. friends opposite in times of national crisis such as the present are very poor tactics. I suggest as well that their tactics of holding up every piece of legislation, important or unimportant, that comes into this house, as they have done, brings discredit on the whole of our parliamentary institutions, for which my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition is always expressing so much reverence. I throw out this suggestion not only for the present opposition but for future oppositions.

My hon. friends laugh,
Mr. Speaker, but it is exactly the same kind of loud laugh that speaks the vacant mind with which they have opposed everything that has been brought down in this house that has been of a constructive nature. I was going to suggest that if we are to protect the interests of the parliamentary institutions in which we believe, then not only at this time but in the future we should endeavour to bring in either closure or some other method of curtailing useless debate of which we have seen so much in the present parliament.
Then, sir, what was the record of the opposition when they were in power? Their record in power was even worse I believe than their record as an opposition. They saw the trading countries of the world barring out our products, and they did nothing to prevent it. They saw the United States by prohibitory tariffs keeping our goods out of that country and they adopted the old attitude of laissez-ifaire, of doing nothing for fear of provoking the United States. When the crash came in 1929 they first denied that there was any unemployment, and they then took the attitude that they would not give a five cent piece for relief even if there was. So far as Beauharnois is concerned, they are still labouring in the valley of humiliation.
In smaller mattere, such as the Montreal bridge, they said it would cost $9,000,000, and it cost $19,000,000. Why did they not when they were in power and conditions were
IMr. Manicm.]
prosperous throughout the world as they were, bring down an unemployment insurance measure which they boast they would support at the present time? Why did they not when they were in power establish a central bank, which now they do not dare to oppose, and which now they say they were always in favour of, but they did not do anything to establish such an institution in the nine years they were in power. They did nothing about farm credits, and nothing about Senate reform, which my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition had clamoured for. They did nothing about free trade. All these things went into the limbo of forgotten things when hon. gentlemen opposite were in power.
So far as the Canadian National Railways are concerned the record of hon. gentlemen opposite in that respect is to my mind the most appalling of all. The hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth, in speaking of the Canadian National Railways, used this sentence:
From 1922 to 1930 the average surplus available for payment of interest due to the public was $24,000,000, and the deficits began again in 1931.
That is one of those half truths in which lawyers so frequently indulge. My hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Bell) says, not the best lawyers. That is probably true. I do not think he would do it, but my hon. friend from Shelbume-Yarmouth did.
The facts are that between 1921 and 1930 my hon. friends opposite in the handling of the Canadian National Railways had eight years out of ten in which there were deficits so far as the interest to the public was concerned. They had a total deficit in those ten years of $191,000,000, and only in two years, in 1926 and 1928, was there sufficient earned by the railways to pay the interest owing to the public on bonds. In those two years they had surpluses totalling six million dollars. That means that they had a total deficit between 1921 and 1930 of $185,000,000 in the handling of the Canadian National Railways.

No, but my hon. friend left unsaid what he should have said to make his statement completely correct. My hon. friend is very clever at that sort of thing, and he is trying to do it again now. He has a clever habit of bringing out only one or two phases of the railway question. He did it in South Oxford, and apparently with good effect. He does it everywhere he goes. He does not tell the whole truth but only one-half or one-quarter and lets it go at that. That is about as close as he got in his statement on the railway question a few days ago.
In regard to interest, let me say that when my hon. friends opposite came into power the amount of interest which the bondholders were receiving from the Canadian National Railways was just $20,000,000 less than it was when they went out of power. In other words, by permitting the Canadian National Railways to go into wild extravagances of many kinds they built up increased interest charges of twenty million dollars a year for that railway in addition to this factor, that the interest to the government was increased in the same period by $12,000,000 per annum by loans and cash advances from the government of my hon. friends opposite. To sum up, they increased interest charges to the public and to the government by $32,000,000 a year in the years between 1921 and 1931.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: All voted for by my hon. friends.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, probably voted for by your hon. friend because my hon. friends opposite had just sat back and permitted the gentleman in charge of the Canadian National Railways at that time to become such a squanderer of the people's money that nobody dared open his mouth for fear of risking his political life. There was no control whatsoever by the government or by the directorate of that day upon the gentleman who later disappeared from the management of the Canadian National Railways, for the good of the railways and the good of this country.
Hon. gentlemen opposite claim to have cut down the debt of this dominion by $257,000,000 when they were in power. That is the figure given by the hon. member for Shel-burne-Yarmouth, and I shall accept it. At the same time they increased the debt of the Canadian National Railways to the public by $161,000,000 so that there was actually an increase in the debt of this country of $204,000,000. Then in the preelection year of 1929 they permitted Canadian National Railway commitments of between $200,000,000 and
$250,000,000 for hotels, terminals, ships and railways, practically none of which was needed by the Canadian National Railways, and which only added to the funded debt of the railway. They encouraged the wildest extravagances. They rolled the Canadian National Railway pork barrel from Halifax, where they built a hotel for my hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth, clear across to Vancouver and back again. They turned the Canadian National into a political machine and a political club of the most severe kind, and they nearly wrecked the Canadian National Railways, and in fact nearly wrecked the country.
That is the Liberal record so far as the Canadian National Railways is concerned during the last nine years in which hon. gentlemen opposite were in power. I say Mr. Speaker, that their record in regard to that great public utility was more appalling than the record of any other government in Canada, federal or provincial, in regard to any public utility this country ever possessed. But now I am happy to say that due to policies of economy, unpopular I admit, and of restriction of expenditure the Canadian National Railways to-day is well and economically managed. It has good officers and men in charge, and it has an efficiency which has been maintained throughout.
Fortunately business for the Canadian National as well as for the Canadian Pacific is increasing at the present time in line with the general increase in business throughout the world. During the months of January, February, March and April of this year the gross revenues of the Canadian National Railways have gone up $9,000,000 as compared with the same four months last year, while the increase in the gross revenues of the Canadian Pacific amounted to $6,000,000. Incidentally, these figures show that the Canadian National is not suffering very much by the treatment of this government. There is another matter which has not been stated before, one of importance and one which I commend particularly to the attention of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan). The number of men working on the railways this last month is 15,000 greater than the number employed three or four months ago.
While the Liberals were in power from 1921 to 1930 they merely floated and drifted along on a world boom tide. They finally tumbled over the abyss in 1929. No signs of wisdom came from them in either the operation or the management of the affairs of this country. No preparation was made for the future when in times like that some

consideration should have been given to the future. Even five thousand years ago in Egypt they prepared themselves during good times for occasional reverses. At the present time the Liberal party is predicting success at the polls but-

speechtext: The hon. member is not apologizing?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend should
apologize for the fact that the whole Liberal party in the province of Quebec was opposed to one man in the city of Montreal who beat

them by 53,000 for the mayoralty. The government in England to-day is made up of the best elements of the Conservative, the Liberal and the Labour parties. That country is muddling through to prosperous days yet in spite of the quality of the government- there is no Liberal party left with the exception of Lloyd George-whenever the government goes to the polls in a by-election they are either defeated or their majority is cut down. The reason for this is the same as the reason for the majorities in the last two or three by-elections in this country. But the hard fact remains that as far as by-elections are concerned, we are one up on my hon. friends on the other side.
The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth has pointed out a fact which he claims to be deplorable. I admit that it is unfortunate that including our railway deficit and relief this country has had to face a deficit in the last year amounting to $135,000,000. This is a serious situation, but I would point out that practically all countries in the world of any importance have had deficits of the same kind. Last year France had a deficit of $375,000,000; Germany had one of $400,000,000; Italy one of $350,000,000; and in June, when her financial year is up, the United States expects to have one between $5,000,000,000 and $7,000,000,000. It has been pointed out that Great Britain had a surplus of $150,000,000, but it should not be forgotten that she did not pay last year the interest on her war debt to the United States, amounting to $182,000,000. Incidentally, we have paid our interest on our war debt. I state this in order to keep the record straight. In order that I may not be accused of misquoting facts, I should like to quote from the budget speech of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Neville Chamberlain. He said:
Neither last year nor the year before did I make any provision for the payment of the war debt to America nor for the receipt of war debts or reparations by ourselves. In the absence of any future development. I propose to follow precisely the same line this year.
The fact remains that instead of having a surplus, the United Kingdom had a deficit just the same as practically every other country in the world. For the benefit of those who sometimes complain of taxation, it is interesting to note that the United Kingdom is the most heavily taxed country in the world. Their ordinary revenues last year-they expect to have about the same this year-amounted to $3,500,000,000. Based on population of 40,000,000, this works out at $90 per head. Our revenues amounted to $271,000,000, or $27 per head.

speechtext: Is that a promise?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friends should
remember that while the population of Great Britain is only four times the population of Canada, the revenues of that country are fourteen times the revenues of this country. Even including the revenues obtained by the provinces, their revenues are eight times as large as ours. Until lately England was considered a free trade country, but her customs collections are six times the amount of ours. Her excise is fifteen times the amount of ours and her income tax, thirty times. They collect thirty times as much in spite of the fact that their population is only four times as great. We in this country know nothing about taxation when we consider the heavy methods employed in England. It is perhaps because of that that England is on the upgrade. I say to my hon. friends who criticize us for our tariff:	Is the business improvement in England because of free trade or is it because of the protection which has been afforded in the last couple of years? I am going to take the opportunity of quoting a few sentences of Mr. David Lloyd George, one of the few remaining members of the practically extinct species of free traders in England. The species is practically wiped out in this country except for the hon. member for Wey-burn (Mr. Young) who claims occasionally to be a free trader. I quote from the Montreal Daily Star of April 28 a cable from Mr. Lloyd George:
We were the first to slump. We claim that we are the first to recover. To what extent is this recovery due to our abandonment of free trade?
And again:
Every free trader would admit that, under the conditions in which the duties were imposed, they were '"bound to act as a powerful stimulant to home industries that were predominantly affected by foreign imports.
And again:
When the world crisis came the universal depression forced producers in every land to sell their goods at any price, wherever a purchaser was to be found. A country without a tariff became a favourite dumping ground. Our imports therefore tended to increase when we were offered goods we needed at the prices of bankrupt stock.
Our manufacturing enterprises necessarily suffered from this eruption of cheap articles. High tariffs arrested this process and home production was bound to benefit as long as the world slump lasts-*
These arguments apply to Canada just as well as they do to the United Kingdom; and in the same way it was just as reasonable for Canada to increase the tariffs of this country along certain lines, for the reasons outlined by Mr. Lloyd George, as it was for Great Britain.
To my mind, and I think in the judgment of all fairminded people in this country, this government has nothing to be ashamed of but much to be proud of. This government, sir, has brought Canada safely through an economic hurricane the like of which has never been experienced before, and, I am sure we all trust, will never be experienced again. The government of Canada now in power deserves, and I believe will get, the gratitude of the Canadian people when the time comes. Canada, as well as the world generally, is on the upgrade; all the indices point to this. Railway earnings, which constitute one of the best indices in any country, are on the upgrade in Canada. Employment has improved; farm and security prices have gone up; construction contracts have increased; automobile, steel, newsprint, lumber and power production have improved; clearinghouse records are higher, and export trade is gaining each month. I am of the opinion therefore that before the election in a year or so the people of Canada will reach the sunlit heights of full prosperity again, and when we go to the country my hon. friends opposite will come back to sit on the same side of the house as they did after the last election.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I first of all extend my sympathies, with those of other members of the house, to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) in the sad bereavement which he has experienced.
I have just listened to a very fiery and fighting speech by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) but I am afraid I cannot enter
The Budget-Mr. Irvine

into his enthusiasm, at least to the extent that he did, in the defence of any administration of the present system or of^any attempt to make it operative. For a long time in this country, even up to the present moment, fiscal policy has been regarded by both parties as the secret of economic advantage or prosperity; that is to say, one party held that we could bring prosperity to Canada by raising tariffs, while the other party contended that we could bring prosperity by reducing them. We have now in office the party that believes in increasing tariffs, and they have been increased; and I am quite willing to admit with the minister who has just taken his seat that in the administration of affairs under a high tariff policy Canada is just as well off as any other country in the world. I do not think there is any question about that, but I add that there is no country in the world that is very well off at the present time. I would even go this far and say that so far as I am personally concerned, it seems to me that so long as we are going to continue with capitalism in Canada I would just as soon see the administration carried on by the present government as by any other government you could pick in the dominion. But I do say that I am opposed to carrying on the present system, and I do not believe that it is possible for any government to administer that system to the satisfaction of the common people.
The next point I want to bring forward is this. We have never had any experience with a low tariff in Canada. We have had low tariff parties but have never had any low tariff practice, so that we are left to guess at what would happen were we treated to low tariffs.
The main contentions of the opposition during this session have centered on two points, first on trade, involving of course the question of tariffs. The contention has been that trade means economic salvation; that tariffs when .they are high prevent trade; that if the Liberal party came into power tariffs would be lowered and we should get more trade, and therefore we should have economic salvation. The next point in their contention has been that the practices of this parliament and of this government have challenged the principle of representative government. These are the two main criticisms that have been advanced this session.
I would suggest that the abolition or the reduction of tariffs in Canada would not necessarily mean a healthy increase in trade. I have pointed out that we have had low

tariff parties and they have never put a low tariff into effect, so that I must deal with the speculative side of the argument, having no practical examples to follow. It may be readily admitted that the tariff is a barrier, but I contend that it is not the only barrier, nor is it the most important barrier. There is in the world to-day in every country what we may call a capitalistic surplus of goods; that is to say, there is a surplus of goods in every industrialized country of the world, over and above that which can be sold or bought at a profit price, and each one of these countries, not being able to consume at home the surplus of goods which machine production has made possible, enters into competition with every other country for the so-called world market, which has been diminishing all through the last century, and has . almost reached now the complete vanishing point.
The time has come when we must insist that the Liberal party, which in its campaign for power holds out promises to the people that it will bring prosperity through tariff reductions, should tell us just exactly how much it is going to reduce the tariff if and when it does come into power. We want to know not only how much the Liberal party intends to reduce the tariff, but on what goods, or whether it intends to reduce the tariff on all classes of goods, or intends to wipe out the tariff entirely. Then we want to know in which countries such proposed tariff reductions will secure for us a market, and for what sort of goods that market will be available. Further, we want to know to what extent that market will be open to us.
These are very practical questions and if insisted on all over Canada they may force the Liberal party, for once at least, to depart from the usual practice of generalizing and making vacuous statements which may be interpreted this way or that but are always interpreted in some other way than the way expected when the pinch comes.
Another point that I want to bring to the attention of the house is that when a nation is in debt, as Canada is, that nation cannot accept the responsibility of meeting its foreign obligations and at the same time ignore the tariff situation in the world as it is. The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) dealt very ably with that point a few days ago. He argued

and I have not heard anyone who has challenged him on that-that a debtor nation must export more than she imports or she will have to default. Some have argued that we can be in debt

The Budget-Mr. Irvine
say to the United States, and export more to Great Britain, and eventually get a favourable balance in the United States indirectly through the clearing house system. But as things are to-day that cannot be done, because all nations have a surplus of goods for export, and nearly all nations are indebted to the United States and trying to do the same thing we are trying to do. I think we may readily concede this point to the contentions of the Liberal party, that goods shipped out of Canada in exchange for goods shipped in should not be subject to a tariff, these things may be, however, better arranged than by tariff policies of the old type. The C.C.F. proposes to arrange that in a scientific way through the appointment of a government board which will handle the export and import trade so that we shall ship goods out only to nations that are in a position to take our goods and give us goods in return or take our goods to apply on debts which we may owe them.
But there is a third point in connection with this contention that a policy of lower tariffs would bring economic prosperity to Canada, that is that, unfortunately for itself, the Liberal party has a record in regard to tariffs which does not inspire confidence. If that party can again prevail on the Canadian people to return it to power once more on the promise to reduce tariffs, after its long years of office in which no attention was paid to that question, then, of course, there is not much hope for democracy.
The next complaint urged against the present administration relates to the preservation of the principle of representative government. I think those who have urged that complaint, particularly with reference to some of the legislation advanced by the administration, have unfortunately mistaken the issue. I venture to say that financial monopoly has been and is a greater danger to representative government in this country than any act which was ever passed by this or any other government. But when the Liberal party was in power it had nothing to say against that financial monopoly, and even at this session of parliament not a word has been uttered that would indicate that they are in any way opposed to the financial monopoly which is in power in all countries. I would say that even the cat with the proverbial nine lives would have been dead long ago if it had been slain as often as the Liberal party affirms that responsible government has been slain in this house. I do not think that there is any reason at all to assume that the present Prime Minister and his cabinet are impairing the principle of
responsible government any more or any less than the government which preceded them.
Let me invite the attention of the opposition to the real challenge to representative government. I have already mentioned the dominating influence of finance, which is not peculiar to Canada but exists in all countries.
I want next to mention the action of the Liberal party itself, which is more dangerous to representative government in my opinion than any legislative proposal. While our people are in debt, while they are unemployed and discouraged, while we have many people in want, the opposition raises hair-splitting points about governmental and constitutional questions. I think that practice has done much to discourage the people of Canada in their belief in representative government, and that the more of that which goes on the less respect will be shown by the people for this house and its deliberations. Take the discussion on the marketing bill which has gone on for the past two weeks, let anyone read that discussion and then ask them how much respect they have for representative government. That is the sort of thing that is doing more harm to representative government than any marketing bill or any act which this or any other government has so far proposed in this house. The Liberal party has failed entirely to present an alternative and constructive program as a substitute for the program that is being carried out by the government in office. This government, however inefficient or ineffective it may have been in dealing with the depression, has at least at this session of parliament given an intelligent response to the situation.

speechtext: They took a long time to do it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As the hon. member says,
they took a long time, but at last they have made an intelligent response. I am not satisfied with that response, I think they should have gone very much further. Neither do I think, as I said at the outset, that this or any other government can under the present economic order prevent unemployment or poverty or debt. I do not believe that can be done by any group of men. I am quite satisfied that the solution cannot be found in any alteration of administration or any change of party or of government; the remedy lies deeper than that, in economic reconstruction on a basis which so far neither the government nor the opposition has seriously considered.
Let me point to a few major facts which concern us in Canada to-day and which should be the basis of our political and

The Budget-Mr. Irvine
economic policy in the near future. The first is the fact of abundance. That has been pointed out from this section of the house many times during the past decade. We have in Canada an abundance of goods and we can produce more. We have potential wealth and real wealth far beyond the ability of the people to purchase. In other words, although we have abundance, that abundance is not distributed. That leads us to the next fact, that devising measures to assure distribution of these goods is the first task of any administration. The third point is that financial reform is the first step to be taken in securing distribution of that abundance. We submit these considerations as the basis of a policy different from that now being pursued by the administration or hinted at in the campaign of the official opposition.
I beg, sir, in resuming my seat, to move, seconded by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman):
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following be substituted therefore:
"This house, while appreciating the unusually difficult task of the government in attempting to administer the present system, regrets the undue delay in taking necessary steps leading to the distribution of our present abundance amongst the Canadian people."

ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the financial critic of the opposition, the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) moved an amendment to the motion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) that the Speaker do now leave the chair and the house resolve itself into committee of ways and means. This afternoon I desire to direct attention to the first paragraph of that amendment. The amendment has been ruled out of order by Your Honour but there is no doubt that it expresses the fiscal policy of the Liberal party and is a public pronouncement made on behalf of that party. The first paragraph reads:
This house regrets that the proposals of the Minister of Finance give no indication of the intention of the government to abandon the policies of economic nationalism which have proved so disastrous to Canada's trade.

speechtext: I would remind the hon. member that the amendment was ruled out of order and therefore is not now before the house for discussion.

speechtext:
Might it not be regarded as a pronouncement with respect to the Liberal party's fiscal policy? It is a public pronouncement made by one of the leaders of the party and I think it gives the people a correct idea of just how the Liberal party itself views the problems of the day. If that is right, then the Liberal party claims the policies of this government have affected the trade of Canada; and if we grant that premise, then it must be only fair and just to arrive at the conclusion that the fiscal or trade policies of the former government affected the trade and the markets of Canada. If, during the term of office of the Liberal party, of which government the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth was a member, our
country lost markets for our agricultural products, then it is but fair to conclude that we were deprived of these markets through the policies of the then Liberal government. The former government must be responsible for any decline in Canada's trade as well as for the loss of markets during their term of office. Therefore I should like to direct the attention of the house and of the country to the lack of policy of the King government, to the lack of effort put forward by the Liberal government from 1921 to 1930 to hold for our farmers an export market for the staple product of the west, namely, wheat. If today we lack a market for our wheat, if any government be involved in the present wheat situation it is the government that held office from 1921 to 1930. The treatment of the wheat market problem by the former administration is a story of the lack of possession of knowledge of wheat market conditions by the members of the then government, or it is a story of the complete ignoring of those conditions, or it is a story of neglect of public duty. I think it is high time the people were told to what extent the King government is involved in our wheat problem, and of its method of dealing with this problem, which it dared not face. It is time we were told that the Liberal government did not perceive the problem and had no policy to offer for the situation. It is time we were told of a government that was weighed in the balance and found wanting in many respects, not the least of which was its attitude towards the wheat situation in 1930 which, as I say, it dared not face but left as one of the many questions to be passed on to the Bennett government for solution.
Our present wheat market situation can be explained only by reference to what transpired before 1930, and particularly by reference to the years between 1925 and 1930. From 1919 to 1925 the countries of Europe, which had been engaged in the war, strove to regain their pre-war production of food products, and by 1925 these countries were then working on a fairly normal basis. European agriculture was therfore fairly well established in 1925, and that continent presented a market picture much different from what was presented to the people, chiefly the exporters, a few years previously.
Canada being an exporter of agricultural products was vitally interested in and would be affected by any policies which might be initiated in Europe. But the King government did not appear to realize the significance

The Budget-Mr. Stewart (Lethbridge)
of the policies initiated in the European countries, and certainly they made no attempt to warn the farmers of the wheat marketing problem which was bound to follow as the results of the policies initiated in 1925 in continental Europe.
Wheat, which is the staple product of western farmers, has for some years been Canada's greatest export commodity, and market trends in wheat have a profound influence on business conditions in this country. When we have good wheat prices business is good in Canada. The transportation of wheat has a direct influence on Canadian business, and the sale of wheat is the largest factor in our export trade. Any policies which might be put into operation which would affect wheat would be of vital interest to the people of western Canada.
From 1921 to 1930, eighty-five per cent of the world surplus of wheat was marketed in the importing countries of Europe but the outlook for that wheat market was greatly changed owing to the agricultural policies which were pursued by those countries in the first post-war years. Germany in August 1925, revised her tariff in an effort to increase the intensity of German agriculture, and the exemption from duty of the most important agricultural products was abolished. In Italy Mussolini in 1925 commenced his famous "battle of wheat," and inaugurated his new policy by placing a duty of 58 cents per bushel against imported wheat.

These three countries, large importers of our wheat, adopted as early as 1925 policies which were designed, (1) to maintain domestic prices, (2) increase domestic production, and (3) limit imports from foreign countries. Through the increase of wheat acreage and through increased production brought about by the use of fertilizers and better methods of cultivation large crops were secured. If anyone is responsible for the loss of these markets surely it must be the gentlemen who were administering the affairs of this country when the tariffs were placed against us.

What action was taken or what policy was pursued by the King government to meet this emergency in 1930? The Prime Minister of the day, in the speech from the throne delivered on February 20, 1930, said:

But listen to this: The then Minister of Railways and Canals, Hon. T. A. Crerar, at his nomination convention in Brandon, held on June 13, 1930, is reported as follows:

I must acknowledge that a spokesman of the then government who attended the League of Nations meeting at Geneva did make a statement either in 1924 or 1926 that the government of Canada was one of the few governments in the world which had kept to lower tariffs at a time when other countries were raising tariffs against her. But when markets are falling away prompt action certainly is necessary. If the action they did take made it so that other countries increased their tariffs against us, then I say that on the face of it that action must certainly condemn them. This country has learned how easy it was under a Liberal government to lose markets, and the present government is finding out how hard it is to regain the markets previously lost.
What policies did the Bennett government adopt to meet these problems that had been left on its doorstep by the King administration? It might have followed the Liberal policy and done nothing but that would bring disaster to Canada in so far as her export markets were concerned. The other alternative, which was adopted by this government, was to face the situation fairly and see what could be done to help the Canadian people in this emergency. What was that policy?
First, an effort was made, and that policy is being followed at the present time, to restore confidence and stability to the domestic wheat market in Canada. The collective credit of Canada has assisted in maintaining an open and continuous market for Canadian wheat, and that in spite of a world surplus, and a Canadian carry-over. Then, in the third place, through the efforts of the right hon. leader of the government the Canadian farmer has been able to secure a market in the largest and most stable market in the world, namely in the United Kingdom. The people will continue to confide in and to repose confidence in the right hon. gentleman who now leads the Conservative party in this House of Commons, the gentleman who during the last four years and in the most troublesome times has presided over the destinies of Canada, a leader who stands among the greatest Canada has yet produced.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the task of speaking in a budget debate is not easy under any circumstances, and when one finds himself compelled to follow so many notable addresses which have already been delivered in this debate and finds that so many phases of the budget have been exhaustively dealt with, it becomes increasingly difficult. It is not without some degree of hesitancy, therefore, that I rise to give utterance to some few thoughts that I have in mind in connection with this budget.
The task of preparing the budget is not an easy one under ordinary conditions, and under the abnormal circumstances in which we find ourselves in this country to-day it is much more difficult. I have often wondered as I have sat and listened during this debate whether it would be possible for any finance minister to prepare a budget which would be acceptable to everyone. Scripture tells us that the day shall come when the laws shall no longer 'be written in tables of stone, but in the tables of men's hearts. I fear that that day will not come until the millennium is with us, and the millennium will have to come before any finance minister in this country will be able to prepare a budget that is acceptable to all. When that time does come, Mr. Speaker, I hope that many hon. gentlemen whose faces I now see opposite will be permitted to remain in occupation of the opposition benches.
I think this much may be said of the present budget speech, that it is a complete statistical picture of conditions as they exist. In most budgets to which I have listened there seems to have been an inclination on the part of the one who prepared it to deal only with the more pleasant features, leaving aside those which were distasteful; but in this particular case I am forced to the conclusion that the

The Budget-Mr. Smith (Victoria)
finance minister has made an honest effort to give to the people a true picture of the country's affairs. The man in the street who can add and subtract can take this budget speech and determine for himself pretty nearly where this country stands.
The duty of any government in my judgment is first to gather in the revenues of the country honestly and to maintain the public services, and to make judicious expenditures that are necessary and in the interests of the well-being of its people. At the present time it becomes necessary for the finance minister in preparing his budget to keep his eye upon the labouring man, who is always worthy of his hire; upon the fisherman, who in his weeks and months of unceasing toil and hardship finds himself on many a day and night labouring and catching nothing; upon the miner, who igoes out to explore unknown territory in the hope of finding untold wealth; upon the farmer, who works early and late in order that he may receive some remuneration from his efforts and have some chance of giving an education and the necessaries of life to the family which he is bringing up. Nor should we forget those who are working in industry. We cannot pay too much regard to these people; for it is necessary and essential that the administration of affairs in this country be so conducted as to provide for the safe investment of wealth so that capital and labour can go forward hand in hand and bring happiness and prosperity and contentment to our people. With the wonderful natural resources that we possess I have no hesitation in saying that if these instrumentalities are bonded together, working in harmony and cooperation, there is no just reason why the people of Canada should not be made a happy and industrious and contented people.
At this particular time we require a government of great courage and determination. I think the very strongest opponent of the present Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Bennett) will have to admit at least that he and his colleagues have displayed since their advent to power a quality of courage which is essential in the momentous and depressing period through which we have been passing. It does not take much of a man to propel a craft when the stream is smooth and he is running with the tide, but in the hour of danger when the tempest arises you need a man of courage, and fortunately for the people of this country during the past three
years we have had such a man at the head of affairs.
Do not let us forget, as so many are apt to forget, that this old world in the last few years has been in cruel agony. We have been pierced with such pains as never before. We have been pierced with social pains, with economic pains, and even with religious pains, and I submit, Mr. Speaker, that we in this chamber, the tried and trusted representatives of the people should try to set aside the prejudices that are so common to politics and by uniting on one platform endeavour to bring about a betterment of conditions in this country which we all love so much.
I said a moment ago that in dealing with his budget the Minister of Finance had been called upon to think of the labourer. I do not believe there is an hon. member in this house who is not sympathetic towards the man who starts out in the morning with a dinner pail on his arm to try to make an honest day's wage in order that he may educate his family, shelter them and give them the ordinary comforts of life. No doubt such a man fills a common position in life, yet after all in many instances the common positions in life are just as hard to fill as are the higher offices for which we sometimes find it very difficult to get men. I said that capital and labour should go hand in hand, and I cannot for the life of me understand a man who is anxious to accumulate wealth while all around him he sees nothing but poverty. I cannot understand a man who can be happy under such circumstances.
Then I speak of the fishermen along the Atlantic seaboard, the gulf of St. Lawrence and the western Pacific. This is a class which endures real hardship and danger. They toil long hours and in many instances for small remuneration. The constituency which I have represented either in the legislature of Neiw Brunswick or in some other capacity for the last thirty years is essentially a farming and lumbering constituency. It will be seen that I started my political career when I was rather young, as I am only a youngster yet.
I should like to submit another matter to this house, if I may be permitted to refer again to myself. A great deal has been said about by-elections and what they indicate as to what might happen in the future. The hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) will remember that in 1927 a by-election was held in my constituency in which a Liberal was elected by acclamation. Two years later the people asked leave to test the constituency and the result was that I was returned to this

The Budget-Mr. Smith (Victoria)
house with the largest majority ever accorded a Conservative candidate. It might be said that by-elections are not a fair index of what the people have in their minds, and I think the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Michaud) will bear me out in that statement. The victory attained by the hon. member who is now sitting in this chamber was not one to be wondered at. That constituency has always been Liberal. If hon. members will look up the records they will see that for the last ten or fifteen years the Liberal candidate in the county of Mada-waska has received almost three votes to every one received by the Conservative candidate.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Even
though there may be a sort of buoyant hope in the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite; even though they may find it necessary to capitalize on this period of depression through which we are passing in order to try to gain the good will of the electorate, I question very much when the time comes for the people to sit down and think seriously on the question whether they will place their confidence in a party which has no policy to submit to them. I shall touch upon this feature later in my remarks,
I stated a moment ago that my constituency was a farming constituency. It runs for a distance of about 150 miles along the international boundary. The principal cash product grown in the constituency is potatoes. Under normal conditions the potato crop of the maritime provinces is valued at about 114,000,000, or twenty-five per cent of the total crop produced in Canada. The former markets for our table stock were the island of Cuba, the United States and the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. These provinces bought freely from us because of the superior quality of the product grown in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. But these markets were closed during the years hon. members were in power. The market in Cuba was closed to us by reason of the high and abnormal duties placed against this product in 1928 or 1929, shortly after a treaty agreement was made with the British West Indies by the former Liberal government. That treaty precluded the possibility of any arrangement being made with Cuba under which we could enter into reciprocal trade relations which would absorb the surplus potatoes grown in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. There are those who say that the present government is mak-
[Mr. B. F. Smith.1
ing no serious attempt to gain access to the Cuban market but if these people knew the facts as they should, they would realize that it is impossible to negotiate with Cuba while the treaty exists between Canada and the British West Indies. I do not say that that treaty was wrong, nor am I stating that the government of that day did wrong in negotiating such a treaty; I say that it was the means of shutting the door absolutely and making it impossible for us to trade or negotiate with a country which had been buying a large part of the surplus table stock of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick.
I am rather surprised at the attitude taken b>' the Liberal members in this house with regard to the farmers. I think it can safely be stated that ever since I came to this house in 1930 the Liberal party has opposed most strenuously every bit of legislation which was brought forward in this chamber to open wider markets for the agriculturists in this country. I mention first the Ottawa agreements. Those agreements were consummated after very careful thought on the part of representatives of all the countries of the British Empire who gathered here and sat around a table for days and weeks; men who were sent here, supposedly because they possessed that degree of intelligence which would qualify them for the duty they had undertaken; men who had a thorough understanding of the conditions prevailing in the different parts of the British Empire which they represented. After most careful thought and deliberation and, as well, in a spirit of cooperation they entered into certain agreements which they believed would enure to the benefit of the British commonwealth of nations.
Now what did we find on that occasion? The liberal party in this house most strenuously opposed those agreements. In spite of the fact that they had been passed in the British House of Commons in a very short time, the Liberal party in this country opposed the agreements, led by the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). I say this with all due respect to the right hon. gentleman-and I do respect him, I must say. I respect him because of the position which he has held as Prime Minister of this country and because of the position which he holds to-day as leader of the opposition, which is one of great responsibility and not an easy one to fill. But I do say that he and his party had very little vision when they attacked the Ottawa agreements, which were entered into, after very careful deliberation with the

The Budget-Mr. Smith (Victoria)
object of benefiting the farmers, of benefiting the lumbermen, the fishermen, the fruit growers and other producers all down the line. One could go on enumerating the different avenues of trade which these agreements were intended to assist. Yet the Liberal party strenuously opposed the agreements, and the leader of the opposition has gone so far as to say on different occasions that if the time ever should come-and heaven knows that I for one hope it never will come-when he is returned to power he will destroy the agreements. In view of the great benefits which we have derived from them in the short time that they have been in force, and what they have meant to the different industries of this country, I challenge hon. gentlemen opposite to take that ground and maintain it when the time for an election comes.
Let me give you some of the words uttered by hon. gentlemen, for I have copied them from Hansard. The leader of the opposition said on one occasion that the agreements constituted a tariff wall around the empire. It was a "Tory conspiracy"; it was undeserving of any support from any quarter. Now what will be the attitude of the right hon. gentleman when it comes to a general election? Let me tell him that he can no longer go into British Columbia and preach one doctrine, into Ontario and preach another, into the maritimes and preach still another. The day has come when men can be heard everywhere over the radio; thank God for that. From one end of the country to the other we can hear the policies they are enunciating in any part of Canada and for which they are asking the support of the people. Well, the leader of the opposition claimed that the treaties were undeserving of any support. But while he was making this declaration, what did the ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) say about them? He declared, as you will find if you will look at Hansard, page 352 of the session 1932-33, that we on this side of the house had "swiped the Liberal policies in broad daylight," to use his own words-and this although the leader of the opposition had just said that the policies embodied in the trade treaties were a "Tory conspiracy." When the vote was taken the ex-Minister of Agriculture voted against the treaties notwithstanding that he had uttered the words I have just mentioned. And the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. McPhee), who gave us such a wonderful dissertation on the budget a few nights ago-

speechtext:
The
hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Sanderson), speaking of the agreements, said that there was nothing in the treaties to give any consolation to the*people of Canada. That was very mild for that hon. gentleman- "nothing in the treaties to give consolation to the people of Canada." But let me go on. The genial doctor who sits in the back seat representing Wellington (Mr. Blair) said that now that he had seen the schedule farms would be for sale because there was nothing in the treaties to help the farmer; and the equally genial member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) declared that the concessions given were vague and illusory. Let me say to my hon. friend that even though the concessions granted might be vague and illusory, it is interesting to look at what has resulted from them. Let me tell him what the result has been. We have had, during the eleven months from April 1, 1933, to February 28, 1934, as compared with the same eleven months in the previous years, an increase in exports to the British Empire of 21 per cent. To the United Kingdom the increase was 20 per cent; to Australia 54 per cent; to British South Africa 61 per cent; to British India 44 per cent. Along with these increases go large increases in exports to foreign countries.
It will be recalled that during the discussion of these treaties it was said that they would make it absolutely impossible for us to mainr-tain our export trade with foreign countries; yet I find that there is a considerable increase in exports to foreign countries, because they are fifty-one per cent higher than they were a year ago. This establishes that the claim of the Liberal party that the treaties would prevent trade with other countries is also wrong.
I think the time has come when every good Canadian is anxious to buy more from the British people and to sell more to them, and

The Budget-Mr. Smith (Victoria)
our import trade is also growing. Compare the imports for February 1934 with those of the corresponding period in 1933. What is the result? Even from foreign countries there is an increase of 41 per cent. From the United States there is an increase of 43 per cent; from China an increase of 31 per cent; from Japan an increase of 39 per cent; from Germany 51 per cent, from the British Empire 45 per cent, from the United Kingdom 41 per cent, from British India 114 per cent, from Australia 182 per cent., and from New Zealand 102 per cent. Thus it will be seen that not only have our exports increased but our imports have increased as well under the trade agreements entered into in Ottawa two years ago.
I think it may safely be said that an honest attempt has been made by the present administration to solve the problem of wider markets. Yet we have had opposition to the marketing act, which I trust will soon become the law of this country. From the very day that bill was introduced it has been met with opposition of the most flagrant kind. Let me say as one who has been engaged in exporting produce on a large scale for the last thirty years, one who has been associated with the shippers of New Brunswick and the New Brunswick Potato Exchange, that many times during that period have we felt the urgent necessity of legislation of this kind to make it possible to carry the products that the farmer was raising and ensure orderly marketing of those products. What are the objections tq this act? In the first place it is urged that it involves compulsion. Well, if the compulsory features were taken out of this bill I would not give a five cent piece for it. Then it is said that these things should be submitted to the House of Commons. We have had the House of Commons here ever since confederation, we have had opportunity to submit to the house questions affecting the farmers, and how far have we got? Hon. members have talked about agriculture being the backbone of this country, but how far have they gone towards assisting agriculture? We assist the railways; we do all we can for the insurance companies and all the rest, but I charge that we have left the agriculturist alone; the attention we have given him on most occasions has been mostly lip service. Now this government have grasped the situation; they have brought down a bill, and placed it before the members representing the farming constituencies. I ask hon. gentlemen opposite how many letters they have received from their con-[Mr. B. F. Smith.!
stituents taking them to task because of the opposition they have offered to this measure; it would be really refreshing to know. It may be that they will have to face the farmers. Let me say that I shall be proud to face my constituents if the time ever comes again, and show them what this government have done and are doing in an honest effort to relieve the distressed condition in which the farmers have found themselves in recent years. We hear a great deal about the distress of the farmers; let me tell you that the farmers in my constituency have been fighting with their backs to the wall for the last few years. They have had a hard time to keep their farms, pay the interest on their mortgages, pay their store bills and keep their families alive. They have not complained very much; they have not asked for bonuses. As far as bonuses are concerned I am opposed to the principle from first to last. I do not believe it should ever have been adopted in this house. Most of the provinces are opposed to that system. The lowering of freight rates to assist the farmers is all right, but when it comes to bonusing any article or commodity of which there is already a surplus it simply stimulates production and the condition is aggravated rather than helped. 1 trust that the time is past when governments will resort to bonusing any article of production, at least any of which we have a surplus.
Yes, our farmers have been fighting with their backs to the wall. We have in my constituency a good many farms that are mortgaged, and the men on those farms find it difficult to pay the interest on the mortgages. Some have borrowed money from the Canadian Farm Loan Board. The Canadian Farm Loan Board was instituted in 1929. The government made available to them 85,000,000 to lend to farmers, and laid down the terms on which loans should be made. I have in my files a list of the loans that have been made by that board since its inception. It is a striking thing that during the last year the loans number just about half as many as in the year before. I have only the statistics to March 31, 1933.
