The Budget-Mr. Smith (Victoria)
I know that it is a difficult matter to lend money on farms, with due safeguards. The utmost care should be exercised in making these investments. But there are provincial boards; every province passed enabling legislation to work in conjunction with the Canadian Farm Loan Board. These provincial boards appoint a superintendent or an inspector, and when an application is made by a farmer an inspection is made and a report sent to the provincial board, which in turn sends its report to the dominion board. I regret to say that during the last year or two, when the farmers of my constituency were really crying for assistance at a time when it meant to them holding their farms rather than losing them, and when they were prepared to offer satisfactory assurance that loans would be paid, the security being more than one hundred per cent, really three times the amount of loan they asked

notwithstanding all this, loans were not available. Let me give an illustration. I know one man who asked for a loan of S600 on a property that under the worst conditions would bring S2,000, and he could not obtain it. I know several instances, which I shall not take the time of the house to cite, in which the Canadian Farm Loan Board has turned down applications for loans from New Brunswick and from my constituency. I am glad to know that the government is bringing down legislation of some kind to help along this line, which shows that this administration is fully alive to the necessity of doing something tangible to assist the farmers, being the first administration to do so in the history of this country. What the farmers want is not money at seven or eight per cent interest; they want to be able to borrow money at reasonable rates, and if the banks can get money from the people at 2 or 2i per cent they ought to be willing to lend that money at one hundred per cent profit at the most. The farmers are the people who should get the benefit of that cheap money, and until they do get that benefit I am satisfied that we shall continue to have deficits on our railways, relief bills and all these other things that would be adjusted if the agriculturists were given a fair chance to obtain that which is their due for the products they produce.
I do not want to refer at length to the tariff, but I- should like to say a word in that regard. Just a few nights ago in this house the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacLean) and the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) took the government to task because they had not relieved the farmers by removing the duty of ten per cent on fertilizer.
Let me tell those gentlemen what that ten per cent means to the provinces of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. We have one plant in East Saint John, operated by the International Fertilizers Company, which covers nearly four acres of ground. Six weeks ago they had a million dollars' worth of chemicals in that building, twenty-seven thousand tons of fertilizer ready to go out to the farmers of Carleton and Victoria counties and even of the state of Maine. Yet these gentlemen would have us remove that ten per cent duty and have that fertilizer mixed in Baltimore, where it was prepared before the ten per cent duty was imposed. The plant to which I have referred gives employment to a large number of men in Saint John; it is one of the most up to date plants in the world, and obtains its chemicals from many different countries. They go to Germany and France for their potash; to Chile for their nitrate of soda; to the United States and the Netherlands for their phosphate, and their sulphate of ammonia is secured in Europe as well. So you see that this is a cosmopolitan establishment. Steamers come there from time to time bringing these ingredients which enter into the manufacture of our fertilizer; the railways are given freight, and we supply not only the people adjacent to that plant but also many people in the state of Maine. If the ten per cent duty were taken off, you would find that the fertilizer would be mixed in the United States, where it was mixed before that duty was imposed.
Let me say further that when the mixed fertilizer came in from the United States it was very difficult for the farmer to know the exact value of that fertilizer, and whether it was composed of the ingredients indicated upon the bag. Now we bring in the chemicals; we mix them there by an up to date mixing process, by which they are thoroughly blended. The fertilizer is dried and put into bags, and shipped out to different parts of the country as well as to the United States. They also have a plant in Prince Edward Island, and this industry means a great deal to the farmers of that province. In the first place they know exactly what they are buying, and they do not pay $75 or $90 a ton for it, as they did originally. The ingredients are brought to Saint John and compounded there; the farmers have an absolute guarantee as to what they are getting, and they buy that fertilizer for $25 a ton.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that a great deal of fault is found with this government by hon. gentlemen opposite.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Would the hon. member
state what commodity was sent to Great Britain?
The Budget-Mr. Harris

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes. The commodity was the leather scrap which is trimmed from hides when the hides are tanned and used for leather of all kinds. There is the pate, the snout, the lip, the ear, the dew claws, the shank pieces and the sinews. I could go into more detail if I were in another place. These commodities are used in the manufacture of photographic film, and that is what I had in mind in the remarks I made. The production in Canada of these raw materials amounts to nineteen million pounds a year, the consumption in Canada about thirteen million pounds a year, and the waste which is now being burned as fuel under boilers or being thrown on garbage dumps, and so on, approximates seven million pounds a year, to my knowledge. That is in answer to the hon. gentleman's question.
I was saying that the physical volume of trade is increasing in Canada. We are also pleased to note that the unemployment figures are getting less and less. I should like to put on record the figures of the international labour office showing that Canada has had a gain in employment of 21 per cent, Japan 11 per cent, South Africa 11 per cent, Sweden 2 per cent, France and Switzerland a decrease each of 1 per cent, Great Britain an increase of 7 per cent. In the United States they have had an increase of 26 per cent. I am very glad to see that increase in employment in the United States. Like others I am very anxious to see that great country prosper and go ahead even with their experimental policies such as the N.R.A.. the A.A.A. and their various codes. It is vital to Canada that the United States should prosper, because we are a population of ten millions living alongside a population of 120 millions. No matter what happens over there we realize that it must have its reaction over here. But, Mr. Speaker, I like the Canadian way of going about the reconstruction of our economic system. We could not afford to carry on the experiments that they have been trying. We have been relying on our experience. We have not shaken the traditions of our people or tried to remould them into	some new form in order	that	we mightlive	and work	out our economic	salvation.You	might say	that we have	just	let thingsdrift. Whether	we did or did	not,	it was far
safer for Canada to travel along the line of experience in the last few years than to launch into a system of experiments such as are being tried on the other side of the line. I am not criticizing the N.R.A., but I have seen the trend of Canada's business shut off from the markets of the United States by the tariffs 
of which my hon. friend spoke. I shall not enumerate them now. But I have seen Canada, a people of ten millions, cut off from a market which they had been supplying to the tune of many millions of dollars, and yet we have survived.
We have been criticized for negotiating a treaty with the motherland. Before I am through I am going to try to convince the house that that treaty was really worth while. I started out to say that we have stuck to the old lines of experience and tradition in the conduct of our affairs. We have avoided launching on such gigantic experiments as are being made on the other side of the line, and what has been the result? While they have their six hour day and their codes and all that sort of thing, the figures up to date show that they have not met their unemployment problem to any greater extent than has Canada. The physical volume of our trade has improved much faster than that of the United States in proportion. We have much less distress in industry in Canada than they have in the United States. Above all, the one factor which has made it possible for Canada to come through this time of stress and strain has been the imperial preference pacts.
The government in power to-day is the poorest group of advertisers that I have seen in this house since I came here twelve years ago. They do not seem to have any idea how to tell the people of Canada what they have really done for this country. They are very poor advertisers, and I say to them now that it is their duty and that of the Conservative party, as I see it, to tell the people of Canada what they have really done during the last three years.
This government has not only maintained the price level but raised it, and it has stayed away from inflation. It has raised the price level by 13-4 per cent in one year, and may I sound a note of warning at this point. In England the price level has been raised by 9-2 per cent; in Canada by 13-4 per cent, and I think that is fast enough.
One satisfactory feature of the rise in wholesale commodity prices in the last twelve months has been that the most of it has taken place in agricultural products. The average rise in agricultural products has been 35 per cent. One product in particular has been spoken about very much in this house; I shall therefore say just a word or two about it. I refer to the hog industry. For the last twenty years there has come to my office

The Budget-Mr. Harris
every morning a full report of what is happening in the Chicago market. Day after day during the last two years I have observed the slaughter of sows and little pigs that are not desirable for edible purposes, until the time was reached when sixteen million were slaughtered and thrown, you might say, into the ash heap. Yet in spite of that, each morning when I picked up the Chicago market reports I see that hogs are selling on the Chicago market and on the twelve western markets at from $3.40 to $3.70, $4, $4.10 and $1.30 per hundredweight, while in Canada the price of hogs has risen in one year from four cents a pound to eight cents.
I wonder if the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. McPhee) is somewhere around the house. Perhaps someone will send a page after him because I am going to say something in a few minutes that he will not think is very kind of me. I will say it now. When that hon. gentleman in a speech in this paper says that not a farmer in Canada has got a copper out of the imperial trade agreements, surely he is stretching the point a little. If the farmers on this side of the border are getting eight cents a pound for select bacon hogs while farmers on the other side of the line are getting only four cents, surely those extra coppers are .going to the Canadian farmer. That shows that the trade agreement has been worth while, and surely my hon. friend from Yorkton is far from the mark when he says that not a farmer in Canada has got a copper out of the imperial trade agreements. I am going to touch further on these trade agreements when he gets down to the chamber if somebody will send for him.
In the meantime, Mr. Speaker, I want to say something about expenditure. Ten years ago, speaking from the other side of the house, I made some suggestions with regard to the .cost of running this country. At that time I thought that we had too much government in this country. I feel the same way about it now. We have too many members in our municipal councils. We remedied that in Toronto during the last year by reducing our city council by nine. We have too many members in our county councils, We have too many members in our provincial legislatures. We remedied that in Ontario by reducing the numbers by some twenty odd. Ten years ago, in 1924, at page 204 of Hansard, I made the observation that I had the pleasure at that time of representing
110,000	constituents. To-day I represent only
80,000. The constituency was cut in half and later increased to 80,000 constituents. I made the suggestion that I was quite willing to endeavour to represent 100,000 constituents in this house. The civil service has been cut by 12,000, in addition to the salary deductions, and if we cut the representation in this house by half we would still be able to govern the country fairly well. When the British North America Act was passed we did not have the radio and there were no automobiles. To-day we can travel ten times as fast and reach a hundred times as many people with the same effort. A number of hon. members could do twice the amount of work they are now doing while a number are doing twice the amount they ought to do. If hon. members would cut out half the drivel they send out of this building and stop half the agitation that is being raised in the minds of their constituents; if they would work full time and serve twice the number of people, we would not be stirring up the people half as much. I am quite serious in this. We are far away from the old days of confederation, and I think there is a great possibility of cutting down the cost of government. We should try to get the people to stop leaning so much on the government. A good deal of the correspondence which goes out of this building is caused by our constituents thinking that the government can do something for them. Individual enterprise and a little sand and backbone will do more for a man than can any government. If I may be pardoned for repeating, with our motor cars and our radios and so on, with the possibility of contact with our constituents, I think each hon. member could represent twice the number of people he is now representing. We would not be bothered with the amount of correspondence with which we now have to deal and the people would not be leaning so heavily on the government.
I think we are all pleased with the trend taken by our trade balances. This balance was unfavourable by $100,000,000 in 1930 while in 1934 it is favourable by $150,000,000. I do not intend to reiterate what the hon. member said just now with regard to the increase in our trade with Great Britain, but inasmuch as the hon. member, for Yorkton (Mr. McPhee) is not yet in his seat, I intend to answer his remarks and he can read it in Hansard to-morrow. He said that not a farmer in Canada has got a copper out of the imperial trade agreements. There are a little more than 10,000,000 people on this side of the water while there are 45,000,000 in Great Britain and 300,000,000 in India. Our trade
The Budget-Mr. Harris

last year increased to the tune of $50,000,000. What was that trade in? Do the farmers of this country know that Canada stands first in the British market with wheat, wheat flour and raw apples? Are these farm products? She stood first in hewn hardwood, zinc, patent leather and rubber boots and shoes. She stood second in oats, hams, live cattle, cheese and manufactured tobacco. Are these farm products? She stood second in sawn hardwood, copper and lead and writing and printing paper. She stood third and fourth and fifth in bacon, canned salmon, hewn softwood, sawn softwood, undressed leather, barley and wrapping paper. My hon. friend has said "not a copper," but I am going to try to illustrate how the imperial preference worked out for Canada last year. He does not seem to understand this matter of dollars and cents so I shall try to illustrate it in another way. The hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Gray) had something similar to say in this connection. In case he does not understand it, I will try to tell it to him in another way. Before I do so, I should like to read a letter I received from Mr. Coats, the dominion statistician. This is dated May 10, 1934, and reads:
In reply to your letter of May 9, the lumber exports which you quote are correct, as are also your deductions.
Here are my deductions. With the excess of lumber shipments last year over the year before to Great Britain you could build a twenty foot board fence reaching from Halifax to Vancouver. If the same excess were used in constructing a wooden sidewalk made of two inch planks, ten feet wide, it would reach from the Atlantic to the Pacific. I ask the hon. member for Yorkton if he can understand that. The shipments of apples under the imperial preference increased from 1,530,640 barrels to 2,983,143 barrels, an excess of 1,452,503 barrels. If a raft were constructed of barrels five in a row and placed on the Ottawa river, it would reach from Ottawa to Montreal. Perhaps the hon. member for Yorkton knows what a raft looks like when it is five barrels wide and reaches from Ottawa to Montreal. That is what the imperial preference did. A steer is anywhere from seven to nine feet long from head to tail, depending upon whether the tail is down or straight out. Shipments of steers to England have increased from five to twenty to fifty-five thousand per year with the help of the imperial preference. If the excess of steers shipped last year over two years before were tied head to tail they would reach from Ottawa to Mont-
[Mr. Harris. 1
real. If the excess shipments of eggs shipped last year over the year before to the United Kingdom were laid side by side they would reach from Ottawa to Halifax. My hon. friend does not understand what a copper is but perhaps he can gain some idea of the magnitude of this shipment of eggs. We have about 22,000,000 laying hens in Canada. If they were placed on this ten foot sidewalk, they would reach from Atlantic to the Pacific. If a gun were fired and they all got the notion and laid an egg at the same time, we would have the number of eggs shipped last year to Great Britain in excess of the number shipped the year before. I see the hon. member for Yorkton has not come in yet. I am trying to talk in his language, because being a lawyer he does not seem to understand what dollars and cents mean. If the cans of fruit and vegetables shipped last year in excess of the year before were placed end to end they would reach from Winnipeg to Halifax. If the copper shipped last year in excess of the year before were made into ordinary No. 14 Browne and Sharpe gauge wire, the ordinary commercial copper wire, it would make 2,074,848,000 feet of wire. It is
25,000	miles around the earth, and this wire would go around fifteen and a half times. Bacon moved from twenty, to fifty, to eighty-three million pounds. Now, if you took all the hogs which it would require to produce that bacon and put them into one corral our friends on the opposite side of the house could not possibly, during the next ten years, make as much noise as they could. If you took that same bacon in the form of breakfast bacon you would have a ribbon of rashers that would go around this world five times. Perhaps my hon. friend from Yorkton does not know anything about coppers, dollars and cents, but at least he will have some idea of the magnitude of this imperial preference, in view of what I have said.
Fifty years hence when some of you young chaps are still here-and I hope the lady member will still be here-you will read in history that in a country called Canada there had been some great achievements. You will read that an act of confederation was passed in 1867 and that later on a national policy was instituted. Still later in a great war Canada did some great things for her mother country, and a little later on in the years 1931, 1932 and 1933 certain trade agreements were initiated with that country. These will be the high spots, and there will be recorded the names of a few men. There will be Macdonald and Cartier, and probably there will

The Budget-Mr. Euler
be mention of the name of Laurier, the man who perpetuated the national policy. History will also record the fact that some speeches were made by some hon. gentlemen opposite who called themselves Laurier Liberals-not Hepburn Liberals or McQuibban Liberals or even King Liberals. It will also be recorded that other people made speeches-people who liked to call themselves Bennett Conservatives. And along with these achievements history will record the names of certain statesmen, among which there will be, in a bright and high spot, the name of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett.

speechtext: I am sure my hon. friend from Toronto-Scar-borough (Mr. Harris) will forgive me if I do not reply to his original arguments so picturesquely expressed. I had no intention whatsoever of participating in the budget debate, and I speak only now because of a certain sense of duty that someone in this house should make a protest at the persistent and continual attacks that are being made not only upon the late government, but also upon the memory of a man who has passed away, with regard to the national railways.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let the dead past bury its dead.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You would like to bury it all right.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It will bury you.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As a believer in the public ownership of the national railways I have always felt that they should be kept out of politics. My good friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion)-I say that sincerely and I think he will take it so-and others, both in this house and in previous meetings of the parliamentary committee on railways, have persistently made charges of extravagance with regard to the railways not only against the King government but against the late Sir Henry Thornton. These statements at the time were perhaps not refuted by some of us as strongly as they should have been. We had a motive in that. For my part I always felt that the attacks that were being made on the railways were made by some at least to discredit public ownership and by others for reasons which I need not give here.
As I say, I have always felt that the railways ought to be kept out of politics if they were to be made a success, and if apparently I trench upon politics the fight is not of my making, because politics was introduced into the debate this afternoon by my friend the Minister of Railways.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No; it was introduced by a number of others who preceded me, the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) among them.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I should like the house to bear in mind that, after all, the constituent parts of the Canadian National Railways as they are now, were taken over by a Conservative government, and the heavy liabilities which we are now carrying, and the heavy interest charges which we find it almost impossible to pay, are the direct result of that action of a Conservative government in taking over the railways some years ago.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You were nine years in power; why didn't you stop it?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is a part of history; you cannot deny it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would point to a statement I made in the house, quoting from Hansard of a good many years ago, when the railways were first taken over, when the right hon. gentleman who is now Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) said that at the time the Canadian Northern was taken over by the government it should have been allowed to go into the hands of a receiver and taken over at a fair price. Perhaps he was right, but apparently his party did not agree with him. But if this had been done, then probably two or three or four hundred million dollars of obligations on which we are now paying interest would not be a burden on the people.
What did we acquire in these railways? We acquired a conglomeration of four so-called railway systems-the Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Grand Trunk Railway and the Intercolonial Railway, which we had already had. I call it a conglomeration of railway systems. Then just as they had been taken over the Liberal party came into power, and they chose Sir Henry Thornton for the great task of welding these railway systems into one great system capable of competing with the Canadian Pacific Railway. I leave it to every member of this house and to the people of this country whether the work he undertook was not a colossal task. He had the duty of coordinating these different railways into one great system. He had to buy a great deal of rolling stock, because on most of the roads the rolling stock was quite insufficient. He had to buy heavier motive power, larger locomotives; bridges had to be rebuilt; and heavier rails had to be laid. And the cost was very considerable. It took hundreds of millions of dollars-regarding which there has been so much criticism-money properly spent.
The Budget

Mr. Euler

to put the system into that condition in which it could compete with the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Sometimes I am almost convinced that the reason why there is so much criticism of the Canadian National Railways is that they were made capable of competing with the great Canadian Pacific Railway. Hundreds of millions of dollars were voted by this house for the purposes of the Canadian National Railways. As has been said before, our friends who are now sitting on the other side of the house and who at that time were on the opposition benches voted for these grants, and without any opposition; and I was surprised this afternoon to hear the Minister of Railways say, when he was challenged on that point, that he had never made objections to voting these large sums of money. Perhaps I am not using his exact words, but this is the sense of what he said. He said it was as much as a member's life was worth to do anything that was in opposition to the wishes of Sir Henry Thornton.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Political life, I said.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

All right; does it mean my
hon. friend places political life above the interests of this country?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

I never admitted they were
extravagances. My hon. friend said they were, yet he countenanced them.

ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I would like to ask in perfect good nature whether that is an example af the red-blooded Canadianism of which he loves to speak.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not need to learn
Canadianism from you.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Millions of ties the year
before election.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will say something about
ties in a moment. Then came the depression. Everyone in the country felt the depression, the railways as all other businesses. Industrial firms had expanded at that time beyond all reason. We all thought-I think I may say that-almost every citizen of Canada, in private life, in business life, in parliamentary life, thought that we had entered upon an era that would be prosperous forever after, and we were all going to be . rich and happy. And then we had the awakening, and the railways did not escape. Every

industry suffered heavy losses: the railways suffered heavy losses. The railways naturally felt the depression in their revenues. They were exposed to greater difficulties than the average business was, for the simple reason that just at that time there became effective the most strenuous competition by trucks and automobiles. My hon. friend said this afternoon, and perhaps quite fairly, that the government should not be blamed so particularly for the difficulties which this country had experienced, because we had been passing through a great world depression. If he claims that justice for the government why does he not do justice in the same way to the railways? The railways suffered through the depression, and it is utterly unfair to blame the railways alone for extravagance in expansion when such blame is just as applicable to every other business carried on in Canada. The great competitor of the Canadian National felt the depression almost as much as the Canadian National itself. That of course was very largely the result of competition. I am not going to weary the house again with my opinions regarding railway competition. As I have said before, competition between the two railways of Canada is not the life of the railways but rather their death.
I want to make just one more reference to the address of the Minister of Railways this afternoon. He referred to political interference with the road while the King government was in power. He made the statement, I think, that the Liberals rolled the pork barrel from one ocean to the other and back again, and that the Canadian National had become a political club. I resent that statement. I happened to be a member of the King government in the last four years of its existence. I cannot recall a single instance while I was a member of that government when any political pressure was suggested in any respect whatsoever with regard to the running of the Canadian National Railways. I knew the late Sir Henry Thornton pretty well. On more than one occasion I asked him whether there was any political pressure brought to bear upon him, and he told me that from the then Prime Minister down he never was subjected to any political pressure by anyone in regard to the running of the Canadian National Railways. I said a moment ago I was not going to indulge in recrimination, and I do not desire to do so, but when the Minister of Railways makes the statement that the late government was exercising political pressure, patronage if you like to use the expression;

The Budget-Speaker's Ruling
that a political club was made of the Canadian National, and that the pork barrel principle was being applied, I should like to say to him and to the house that these words come ill from the mouth of the man who said in the committee two years ago that out of twenty-eight tie contracts, twenty-seven were switched by him to Conservatives.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I did not say any such thing.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is on the record. Now I have nothing more to say. I have tried in my feeble way to defend the memory of a man who is gone, a man who, I believe, did a great service for this country. He had the defects that great men often have. But I should like to close by suggesting that if we must fight partisan battles with regard to the condition of the Canadian National, let us at least allow to rest in peace a man who while here never was properly able to defend himself, and now is not able to defend himself at all.

speechtext:
A resolution was moved on the 5th of February, 1934, and adopted by the present government, the last words of which are as follows:
-in order that they may absorb the goods produced, thereby creating a more equitable distribution of our wealth production.
The government officially accepted the details of that resolution, and it was unanimously adopted by this house. I submit with great respect that the words in the amendment now moved referring to the distribution of our present abundance are merely a repetition of the resolution adopted by the house on February 5, 1934.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The amendment moved by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine), seconded by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman), reads as follows:
This house, while appreciating the unusually difficult task of the government in attempting to administer the present system, regrets the undue delay in taking necessary steps leading to the distribution of our present abundance amongst the Canadian people.
It is now alleged by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) that the amendment is out of order on the ground that the matter therein dealt with was disposed of by a motion made by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) on February 5, which motion reads as follows:
Whereas there still exists in Canada an acute unemployment problem, and
Whereas it is desirable that as many as possible of these unemployed should be absorbed into the industrial life of the nation;
Therefore be it resolved, that, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into immediate consideration the necessity of reducing the hours of labour of those engaged in industry, and also increase the purchasing power of the masses of our people in order that they may absorb the goods produced, thereby creating a more equitable distribution of our wealth production.
That motion was agreed to. The principle thereby enunciated was adopted by the house. The amendment now before the house does not propose a policy or advocate the adoption of a principle; it merely regrets the undue delay in taking necessary steps leading to the distribution of our present abundance amongst the Canadian people. It is merely a statement of regret that the principle adopted in the resolution of Mr. Heaps of February 5 is delayed in its execution. I therefore hold that this amendment is in order.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to delay the vote in the house, and I should not have risen except for the language of my hon. friend (Mr. Euler) in accusing me of attacking the memory of a man who is dead.

I criticized the late government and I criticize them now for their absolute neglect of public duty in permitting the management of the Canadian National Railways to spend the huge sums that they spent on useless appurtenances to that railway, such as hotels, scattered from the Atlantic to the Pacific-

speechtext:
Did you ever make a
protest?

The Budget-Mr. Manion

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that hotel was the result of an agreement which was made before Sir Henry Thornton came in.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not that hotel.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not for a hotel, but for something else.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The so-called shadow government concluded that agreement with the city of Vancouver and agreed to build a hotel costing $3,500,000. My hon. friend and his government increased that sum until it

reached $11,000,000, and the contracts were let before we came into power. They purchased railway lines all over the east, not one of which ever paid operating expenses. They built ships costing over $8,000,000 to compete with the Canadian Pacific ships, when the Canadian Pacific were not making any money. These ships which cost $8,000,000 now are rotting away because there is no work for them. In all, in these items I have mentioned, they spent at least $150,000,000 that was absolutely wasted, not one cent of which was justified, but which was merely added to the capital expenditures of the Canadian National Railways. They added probably something like $8,000,000 or $9,000,000 a year to the bonded indebtedness of that railway.
But that was not all, Mr. Speaker. That was in a preelection year. My hon. friend suggests, in that high minded manner which he adopts here and in other parts of this country, that he was too honourable to permit any money to be spent on politics by the Canadian National. I say that entire amount of $150,000,000 was spent on politics. I believe I am justified in saying that the Liberal party permitted the pork 'barrel to roll from the Atlantic to the Pacific and back again for that purpose. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, there was an amount of $600,000 placed in the estimates of 1929 for a hotel in Prince Rupert, a little place of fifty-five hundred people, where you could not build a $25,000 hotel and make it pay. That $600,000 hotel was provided for in the estimates of 1929, and we had to stop it.
That is only part of it; all through the Canadian National Railways, when we came into power, there were ridiculously high salaries. Just let me quote some of the salaries that were being paid. Mr. Gaston was receiving $62,000 a year, and my hon. friend was a minister in the government that paid that amount out of the taxes of the people of this country. That man was receiving $62,000 a year for doing nothing that was useful to the country or to the people. Those who came to me asking that we should get rid of Mr. Gaston were the officers of the railways themselves, not Sir Henry Thornton. The officers of the railways pointed out to me that Mr. Gaston was lording it over the rest of the men, without doing a cent's worth of work for his $62,000 a year. There were other men getting from $45,000 a year down; ninety-six of them were paid over $10,000 a year. Imagine that, Mr. Speaker; there were ninety-six employees of the Canadian National 'Railways receiving

The Budget-Mr. Manion
over $10,000 annually when the Canadian Pacific had only fifty-three employees receiving more than that amount.
Then let me say a word with regard to specifications. My hon. friend put himself out to taunt me because at one time I spoke of red-blooded Canadianism. Well, Mr. Speaker, I do not think I need learn anything about Canadianism from the hon. gentleman, at any rate. Laying that aside for the moment, however, the hon. gentleman was a member of the government which permitted the late management of the Canadian National Railways to specify that forty per cent of all the material supplied for the Saskatoon hotel, the Halifax hotel, the Montreal terminals-that $50,000,000 extravagance which was absolutely unnecessary-should come from the United States. He was a member of the government which permitted the Canadian National Railways to spend $100,000 a year on club dues, which now have been cut to something between $5,000 and $10,000 a year. He was a member of the government which permitted the Canadian National Railways to spend $2,000,000 a year on entertainment account, which now has been cut to something like $400,000 a year or less. He was a member of the government which permitted the Canadian National Railways to switch accounts. They would pass millions of dollars for the construction of such useless appurtenances as the Saskatoon hotel, for example, or the Vancouver hotel; then, at the whim of some individual in the Canadian National, they would switch those amounts. They did that in 1930 to the extent of $8,000,000. He was a member of the government which permitted the Canadian National Railways not only to spend money in this country but to go down to Jamaica and start to build a hotel there, which was estimated to cost half a million dollars but which actually cost a million dollars. This hotel cost the people of Canada $270,000, and today it is nothing but a bone of contention between the people of Jamaica and the people of this country; it has been of absolutely no use to the Canadian National or to the people of this country, yet it cost us $270,000. My hon. friend was a member of the government which hired Sir Henry Thornton at a salary of $75,000 a year and legitimate expenses, which were estimated at about $25,000 annually. Yet he was a member of the government which permitted Sir Henry Thornton to draw $150,000 year after year, and at least $50,000 or $60,000 of that amount had no real basis. My hon. friend was a member of the government which permitted Sir Henry Thornton, in addition, to take over the house in which he was living, a house for which he paid $5,000 or $6,000 a year, but which, after it was taken over by the management of the railways, cost the Dominion of Canada $20,000 a year.
I have a whole list of items of extravagance here; I could go right on down the list. There is the radio, for example, which cost over $250,000 a year, but which was of no use to the Canadian National Railways. Yet my hon. friend says he was not acquainted with any reason why he should have interfered, or something to that effect.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I never said that.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My hon. friend says he knew of no unfair extravagance, or political interference. There should have been political interference, if there was not; there should have been some interference to get the Canadian National back to where it is now, under economical management, which is fair to the country and to the railway itself.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is there any political interference now?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
To the extent of keeping them on an economic and decent basis, yes; there is political interference to that extent, and God knows it was needed, when we came into power. All one has to do is look at the Duff report, extracts from which I have before me. Speaking of the Canadian National under the regime of my hon. friends the Duff report says:
Running through its administrative practices, however, has been the red thread of extravagance.
I could go on and quote statement after statement of that kind from the Duff report, which was brought in by men who were fair judges, business men who had no axes to grind and no political favours to give, men who looked over the whole Canadian National system and gave a fair-minded report. They condemn most severely the attitude of the Canadian National, and without putting it into so many words, though in some places they get very close to it, they condemn my hon. friend and his government for permitting the Canadian National to carry on these wild extravagances to the extent I have indicated.
So far as Sir Henry Thornton is concerned, I merely wish to close1 on this note: I have never attacked Sir Henry Thornton personally; I have attacked the extravagances of the Canadian National Railways and I think rightly so, as any man in this house has a per-

The Budget-Mr. McGibbon
feet right to attack such extravagances, feeling that 'he has a duty to perform towards this country. If I never perform another duty for Canada I think I have performed a good one in cleaning up the mess that my hon. friend and the government of which he was a member left so far as the Canadian National Railways were concerned, and with which I had to deal after they went out of power.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Question.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after serving seventeen years in this House of Commons I am not to be silenced by a demonstration of this kind.
I think I may leave it to the judgment of the house whether I have spoken very often during this or any other session. I rise now not because the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) needs any defence, but to protest against the speech of the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler).
As most hon. members know, a few years ago I had something to do with exposing the extravagances, and I believe I am discreet in my language when I say that I helped to expose the graft, which were found at that time in the Canadian National Railways. Ever since, in this house and on the public platforms, I have refrained from exposing the knowledge which came to me from investigations I was called upon to make during that time. I have been content-yes, I have been willing in the interests of this great nationally owned enterprise, to let bygones be bygones, and to devote all the talents and the ability I possess to the building up of the fortifications of public ownership behind this great enterprise. But when year after year I hear charges made that we are out to destroy the national railways, and when I heard the hon. member for North Waterloo speak to-night, as he has spoken in the country in weeks gone by, and when I noted the tone in which he spoke, I believed it my duty to rise and to protest. I want to tell him and to tell this House of Commons that if hon. members want me to expose what I know and that which up to the present I have not exposed, namely the graft that was carried on in the national railways, I am willing to take the people of this country into my confidence, and to tell them what I found out.
The hon. member who has just spoken was appointed, with myself, to go to Montreal and to investigate the railway accounts. Did he go? No, he refused to go. Every member on the Liberal side of the house refused to go. In fact, only one hon. member, namely the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. MacMillan),

had the courage to go down there and to investigate the accounts of the national railways. I want to say here and now without fear of successful contradiction that what we found there was a disgrace to the executive of any great corporation. I have not said so before, but I am prepared to say so now either in this house or in the country.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does not the hon. member think that as a member of parliament it was his duty to expose graft, no matter where he saw it?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If it is my duty it is equally the duty of hon. members sitting opposite, but they failed to do it. You would not do it, not one of you.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They are not detectives.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You might, then have given some assistance to those who were willing in the interests of the people of Canada to play the part of detectives.
I want to go back to the beginning of the national railways question. Where did it begin? I repudiate the suggestion that it was begun by the Conservative party. I say it began first when the bonds of the Canadian National Railways from Fort William to the east were guaranteed, and again at the beginning of the building of the Transcontinental railway from Winnipeg to Moncton. After those two things had been done by a Liberal government, the national railways became a question for the parliament of Canada, and for no other body. You cannot get away from it. I was a member of the house when, in 1919, the railways were taken over. What did we find? It is quite true that some of the railways threw up their hands and said, "We are through." But that did not relieve the parliament of Canada from its obligations. Read the railway history of that time and see what you find. The parliament of Canada at that time had obligations amounting to $331,000,000 to which they had put their name and which they would have to pay. In addition to that the provinces had guaranteed $96,000,000 worth of bonds. 'In addition to that we had another $400,000,000 invested in railways like the Intercolonial. In other words, something over $800,000,000 which Canada then had at stake 'would have been lost if we had let the railways go into bankruptcy. It is all very

The Budget-Mr. McGibbon
well after the fact to say, "You should have done so and so," but at that time the Dominion of Canada and the provinces would have lost practically $800,000,000, had we done so.
What happened? We took over the railways. What did they cost the people of Canada? They cost about another $800,000,000, and in that we had the whole Transcontinental system, we had the terminals, we had the gathering lines and everything that is essential to a railway system. When we went out of power what happened? What happened between the day we went out of power in 1921 and when we came back in 1930? Read the Duff report, and you will find that during that period $922,000,000 of debt was placed upon the railways, through the instrumentality of the King government; $922,000,000 more was added to the debt. That is the condition with which this government was faced when it came into office. You want to know why? Well, just look at some of the railways which were taken over. Take, for example, the Gaspe railway. I am told that the year before last it cost a million dollars to take the snow off that line. What about the Quebec, Montreal and Southern railway? Read the reports prevalent about that deal, where the vendors sold for $6,000,000, and only $5,000,000 reached the owners. Read those reports. Then, read the reports of the extravagances exposed in the committee which sat in this building; read about the deals in New York, the offices in that city and, as the minister suggested, the extravagant salaries. Consider the commissions on everything bought for the national railways, and the extravagance in connection with the building of branch lines. Compare the expenditures on the Canadian National Railways with those of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and you will understand how through extravagance the cost mounted up year by year. Consider the hotel competition, and the fact that the hotel in Saskatoon cost $16,000 per room. Is it any wonder it has never been opened? I placed on the committee records an agreement drawn by the late Doctor Reid, then Minister of Railways, indicating that the government of the day was exempt from all obligations in connection with the building of a hotel at Vancouver. At one time there were obligations, but through negotiations he exempted the government of the day from those obligations. Yet the building of the hotel was proceeded with, and the railways, through the government of the day, authorized a building
costing $11,000,000. Is it any wonder that the national railways got into the mess in which we found them when we took office?
I want to tell the hon. member for North Waterloo that the government of which he was a member has damned public ownership through the instrumentality of the national railways for all time to come in the Dominion of Canada. I say without fear of successful contradiction that the national railways cannot be made to pay, and when I say that I am wiping off the $1,300,000,000 of Canadian government obligations. I take into consideration only the $1,253,000,000 of bonds that were put out to the public and on which we have to pay something like $58,000,000 of interest a year. In my opinion the day will never come when the national railways can break even and pay their debt to the public. It cannot be done, and I would ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), I would ask parliament and the people of Canada this question: Is it not time that we faced this situation as we ought to face it, as a business proposition? If we cannot do anything better let us say to the people of Canada that in our judgment these two railways should be united. I said that a year ago on the floor of this house, and I was glad to read in the press only the other day that Mr. E. W. Beatty recently made practically the same speech to his directors that I made a year ago on the floor of this house. If we can save $75,000,000 a year, as the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway says we can, as the hon. member for North Waterloo says we can, and as the late president of the Canadian National Railways said we could, why not do it? Why continue to ask the people to put their hands in their pockets year after year to raise fifty or sixty or seventy million dollars, -for what purpose? To finish paying for the national railways? No. The people do not own the national railways, and it is only a fallacy to think they do.
I remember the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) asking the late Sir Henry Thornton what value he would put on the national railways as a going concern, and he replied about sixty thousand dollars per mile. If you figure that out it means just the amount of money that we owe the public. That is all they are worth, and all we are doing is holding the bag. Are we going to continue to ask the people of this country to put their hands in their pockets year after year and pull out fifty or sixty million dollars? And remember, that does not take into
The Budget-Mr. McGibbon

account any depreciation; it allows nothing for improvements, extensions or betterments.
As I have said before, if we are going on with these roads as they are to-day, they will cost this country $75,000,000 a year for many years to come, and what do we get in return? Surely with the competition there is to-day from buses; with the competition which is in sight from the air, and with the control which the board of railway commissioners exercises, this country is sufficiently protected against a railway monopoly. Surely we do not have to spend sixty or seventy million dollars a year simply to protect this country against a railway monopoly. I say without fear of contradiction that taxation will have to be lifted from the back of the individual and from the back of business before this country can regain that degree of prosperity which we are all hoping for.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend a question?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If you do not make it too hard.

speechtext: My hon. friend is suggesting amalgamation, as I have done before. Would he have amalgamation under private or public, ownership?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am glad my hon.
friend has asked that question. I was going to say that the Prime Minister should let the people decide that question by referendum. Let them say whether they want these roads run under public or private ownership. I have no hesitation in saying that I would choose private ownership, but the people have such a huge investment in these roads that they have a right to be consulted. I would say to the Prime Minister:	Work out a scheme
of amalgamation. I mean more in the line of what I suggested a year ago, namely, that the government retain ownership of its own lines and the Canadian Pacific Railway retain ownership of its lines, but put them under joint operation and let the people decide whether they be under public ownership or private ownership. But for goodness' sake let us relieve the people of the heavy financial responsibility they are carrying to-day and which they must continue to carry unless something is done.
I was dreadfully disappointed when I read the other day Mr. Beatty's statement that only one million dollars' worth of savings had been effected through cooperation in one year, and presumably the greatest savings have already taken place. Now when we are faced with a deficit of $65,000,000 or $70,000,-

000	a year on account of the national railways
1	ask this parliament what right have we to inflict that taxation on the people when there is a remedy for the situation? I ask the Prime Minister and I ask this house to submit this question to the people of Canada in an unbiased way with the idea of consummating amalgamation of these two roads so far as operation is concerned, and let the people say whether they want it done under public ownership or private ownership.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few remarks before the main motion is put, I think we have witnessed something which is typically characteristic of the previous and the present governments. I refer to the sane, logical and reasonable remarks of the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) as compared with the utterly partisan, bombastic and venomous remarks of the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion). The minister referred to the extravagance of the previous government, but I do not think there was ever anything so extravagant in connection with any government in this country as the remarks he made. It is not my intention
to occupy the time of the house at any length as we are all hoping to get to a vote on the main question, but in view of the fact that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) has been ruled out of order, I desire to move an amendment which I submit expresses in a very few words the views which have been expressed wherever an opportunity of expression has been afforded in recent months in any riding in this country. I submit that this amendment represents the general feeling of the people of Canada at the present time. I beg leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot):
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be omitted and the following be added instead thereof:
In the opinion of this house the present administration no longer enjoys the confidence of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my understanding of the rules of this house is that only one amendment and one subamendment can be moved to the main motion that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair. During the present debate an amendment was moved and declared out of order. Subsequently a subamendment was moved and also declared out of order. Another amendment was moved and has been voted upon but no subamendment was moved. I submit that under rule 49 no further amendment is permissible. If it were otherwise we might be met with amendment after amendment as votes are taken, and Your Honour would never be permitted to leave the chair. There are other reasons why this amendment is out of order, but at the moment this is my principal reason for objecting.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Standing order 49 reads:
Only one amendment and one subamendment may be made to a motion for Mr. Speaker to leave the chair for the house to go into committee of supply or ways and means.
That would seem to prevent the present amendment being in order, and I rule it to be out of order.

We are dealing with
foreign insurance companies. The method is somewhat technical. Certain decisions

have been arrived at in the privy council since 1916 to' date, and it is believed that this legislation will clarify to some extent the difficulties that have been experienced. It is complementary to a bill that follows on the order paper. speechtext: If the house gives second reading, I am sure the Prime Minister will agree that it is on the understanding that we may discuss in committee everything which we might discuss on the second reading.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: FOREIGN INSURANCE COMPANIES
speechtext:
I judged that that was what the right hon. the leader of the opposition intended by his question; I construed it

Foreign Insurance Companies
as such. If the house gives the second reading,
I do not propose that it should limit its right to discuss every feature of the bill, even though that might involve some question of principle.

subtopic: FOREIGN INSURANCE COMPANIES
speechtext:
Mr. Bennett, for the
Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes), moves that Bill No. 50, entitled an act to amend the Foreign Insurance Companies Act, 1932, be now read the second time.

subtopic: FOREIGN INSURANCE COMPANIES
speechtext: What is the advantage in that? My right hon. friend says that it is for the purpose of having the bill circulated. Surely the bill may ibe circulated before the second reading. Bills are always printed and distributed before the second reading. Why the change in this instance?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: FOREIGN INSURANCE COMPANIES
speechtext: The former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) is entirely correct. The bill has to be printed in English and French before it is given the second reading. I should have said, more properly, that the official presentation of the bill for the consideration of -members arises by reason of its being given second reading, and the house is then in a position either to discuss the details of the bill in committee of the whole house or to send the bill to another committee. I intended to move the bill one step forward to-night. Perhaps the language I used with respect to the necessity of its being printed was too wide.

subtopic: FOREIGN INSURANCE COMPANIES
speechtext:
I fail utterly to
comprehend why this bill should be given special treatment, different from that accorded other bills. Apparently it is not because it should be printed, because there is nothing to prevent its being printed and circulated before the second reading, and we have not been given any details with regard to the principle underlying it. I do not like advancing the bill at this -time, making in this way an exception of it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: FOREIGN INSURANCE COMPANIES
speechtext:
The rules of the house do provide that on the second reading of a bill it is not proper to deal with the several sections. This bill is one which amends the existing sections of a statute, and the extent of the amendments is indicated in the bill. The reason it has to be printed in English and French before it is read -the second time, as the hon-. gentleman has said, is that members may at least see it. The principle of the bill is merely to amend and make more perfect existing legislation which was passed at a previous session and with respect only-so far as this bill is concerned-to foreign insurance companies, with respect to which the
legislative jurisdiction of this parliament is unquestioned. If this were a new measure and I were asked to unfold to the chamber the principles involved in it, I would do so, but where it involves merely amendments, according to the rules it is not sound parliamentary practice to take the bill section by section and indicate at this time what is involved. If I say that the principle of the bill is to make more perfect the administration of this statute I have said all that is involved with respect to it, as any one can see by taking a casual look at it.

subtopic: FOREIGN INSURANCE COMPANIES
speechtext:
I submit that all this discussion has been completely out of order, because, sir, you were reading the motion for the second reading of the bill, and I understand that on the second reading a member can speak only once. The Prime Minister spoke several times, and other members also. I submit, sir, that this discussion is irrelevant and out of order.
Now, speaking on the second reading I have just one word to say. Lloyds will be very much surprised when they see this legislation and learn for the first time after centuries that they are called an insurance company. For the benefit of the government may I tell them that if they will glance at the Encyclopaedia Britannica in the library they will see that Lloyds is not an insurance company; it is just a club.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FOREIGN INSURANCE COMPANIES
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit me? He is confounding this bill with the one which immediately follows it. This bill deals only with foreign insurance companies. The next bill deals with British and Canadian companies.

subtopic: FOREIGN INSURANCE COMPANIES
speechtext: I thank the minister for his explanation. I am glad to hear that this bill does not refer to Lloyds as an insurance company; and what the Minister of Justice has just said confirms what I said before.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Sullivan in the chair.
On section 1.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: FOREIGN INSURANCE COMPANIES
speechtext: It will be observed that the only change is that in the original preamble the words were "soliciting and securing." It is proposed to change it to "are soliciting applications for and issuing," so as to conform to the facts, namely that they are soliciting applications for and issuing life insurance policies. That is the only change in that section.

Section agreed to.
Questions
On section 2.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: FOREIGN INSURANCE COMPANIES
speechtext: This is changing one word only, as to the extent of the insurance at risk, it having been stated as "three and a quarter billions of dollars" when the other statute was passed, and now being "four and a quarter billions" or thereabouts.

Section agreed to.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Bennett the house adjourned at 10.50 p.m.
Wednesday, May 16, 1934
